content: The following entities are responsible for monitoring and implementing health workforce policies: national and regional ministries of health, professional chambers, institutions or units tasked with health workforce monitoring, the Ministry of Labour, and the National Statistical Office. Additional information and references can be found in WHO publications from 2005, 2008, and 2015, as well as the EU Joint Action on Health Workforce Planning and Forecasting (2015). The ability of a Human Resources for Health Information System (HRHIS) to generate data for tracking entrants into the health labor market is an important indicator. This indicator is associated with collecting data on labor market entry flows, as outlined in Module 05 of the Health Labor Market Flows framework. By 2020, all countries were expected to have made progress in establishing registries to track health workforce stock, education, distribution, flows, demand, capacity, and remuneration. Key questions to assess this indicator include whether a system exists to provide information about the health workforce and whether it tracks inflows into the health labor market. The HRHIS should also be capable of generating data to track the active stock of the health labor market. This indicator relates to collecting stock data for labor market entry, as described in Module 01 of the Active Health Workforce Stock framework. By 2020, countries were expected to establish systems to monitor health workforce stock, education, distribution, flows, demand, capacity, and remuneration. Questions to evaluate this include whether a health workforce information system exists and whether it provides data on the stock of the health labor market. Another critical capability of the HRHIS is to track exits from the health labor market. This indicator is linked to collecting flow data for labor market entry, as outlined in Module 05 of the Health Labor Market Flows framework. By 2020, countries were expected to have systems in place to monitor health workforce stock, education, distribution, flows, demand, capacity, and remuneration. Questions to assess this include whether a health workforce information system exists and whether it provides data on outflows from the health labor market. The HRHIS should also be able to generate geocoded information on the location of health facilities. This indicator is related to collecting distribution data for labor market stock, as described in Module 01 of the Active Health Workforce Stock framework. By 2020, countries were expected to establish systems to monitor health workforce stock, education, distribution, flows, demand, capacity, and remuneration. A key question to evaluate this is whether a health workforce information system provides geocoded data on the location of health workforce activities. The National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) indicators were developed through a stepwise process involving consultations with experts worldwide. Over 450 indicators were initially selected from various international and subregional sources, which were then filtered to a set of 255. This process aimed to eliminate duplicates while ensuring all relevant data concepts were included. A global consultation in 2015 involved over 70 experts who evaluated the indicators based on relevance, availability, and national utilization. The final list of indicators was defined through discussions and workshops at WHO headquarters. The NHWA system is built on existing tools, such as the WHO minimum data set for health workforce registry (MDS), the Joint Questionnaire on non-monetary health care statistics by OECD, Eurostat, and WHO, and the European Union Joint Action on Health Workforce Planning and Forecasting. These tools aim to minimize data collection duplication while enabling integrated data analysis for policy development. Examples of NHWA applications include assessing the self-sustainability of the health workforce, addressing geographical imbalances in workforce distribution, and evaluating health worker training performance. For instance, self-sustainability occurs when national production compensates for workforce losses and adapts to population needs. Geographical distribution monitoring helps address imbalances, particularly in underserved areas, supporting the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health 2030. Training performance is critical for ensuring a sufficient supply of new health workers, with milestones such as establishing accreditation mechanisms and improving course completion rates. The NHWA indicators are disaggregated by occupation, using the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-08) where possible.
